theory.text: Matching Information asks which paragraph contains a given piece of information. Matching Features connects statements with a named person, place or other category. Check whether letters may be used more than once.
Key skills: Scanning names and concepts; matching paraphrased relationships.

guide.text: Identify what must be matched  scan for distinctive terms or names  read contextual evidence  check meaning, not just keywords  follow reuse instructions.

small.text: A. Dr Lin measured rainfall. B. Dr Rao compared soil samples. C. Dr Park designed water sensors.
Match the descriptions with A–C: E1. developed measuring equipment; E2. studied soil; E3. collected precipitation data.

full.text: A. In 2015, the city converted an unused railway line into a footpath for commuting and exercise.B. In 2018, engineers installed rain gardens beside streets to absorb stormwater.C. In 2021, a university surveyed cyclists and pedestrians about which routes felt safest.
Which paragraph contains the following information?1. A study of users’ perceptions2. An old transport route put to a new use3. A method of managing excess rainfall

Dr Amelia Green studied how trees could reduce temperatures in crowded city centres. Her findings suggested that shaded streets stayed cooler in summer.Professor Daniel Brooks examined traffic noise and found more frequent sleep disturbances among people living near major roads.Dr Sophia Chen investigated recycled materials in public buildings and reported that some could reduce construction costs.

Match statements 1–4 to researchers A–C. You may use a letter more than once.A. Dr Amelia Green    B. Professor Daniel Brooks    C. Dr Sophia Chen1. Investigated vegetation and urban temperatures.2. Studied transport noise and sleep.3. Examined ways to reduce building expenses.4. Found a benefit of shaded streets during summer.

rows: Green studied trees and city temperatures.
Brooks researched traffic noise and sleep.
Choosing FALSE when evidence is missing
Use FALSE only if the passage contradicts the statement; otherwise consider NOT GIVEN.
Choosing a heading because one word matches
Summarise the paragraph’s full main idea.
Answer using the evidence in the passage only.
Recheck NO MORE THAN ... WORDS instructions and spelling.
Check the complete sentence against evidence.
Spending too long on one question
Move on and return after easier questions.
Confusing a quoted opinion with the writer’s stance
Identify who holds the opinion before answering YES / NO / NOT GIVEN.
Filling a gap with an unsuitable word form
